catalog_quote: 1.2.1. Stress Lexical stress generally falls on the first syllable of the root and on alternate syllables. Every word receives at least one stress except monosyllabic particles (clitics), where it is optional, as in (2b). In addition, stress falls on heavy syllables, which have VV or V' as their nuclei, wherever they occur in a word, as in (2d). Phrasal stress generally falls on the last syllable of the phonological phrase, usually marked with a rise in pitch, and this rule may supercede the lexical stress rule. Syllables preceding heavy syllables or final syllables may lose stress, as in (1b) and (2a). Lack of stress may condition other phonological changes (cf. §1.3.8.3, §1.3.8.4). Variation in stress may be due to the variation in speakers' phonological phrasing and may involve conflicts between the principles of lexical and phrasal stress. When the phrasal stress rule conflicts with…
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: Stress. We have practically no information on the location of stress in Itza. The following citation from Schumann (1971:35) is one of the few direct references to stress, and it is not very helpful: Stress has a rather varied function. When a word is uttered in isolation, the stress always falls on the final syllable. In context, the stress of a given word varies according to the intonation which the utterance requires, but if emphasis is desired, the stress is kept on the final syllable. At any rate we can infer that there is a strong tendency to stress the final syllable of an utterance (be it a single word or a string of words).
new_statements.citation: Dienhart, John M. 1986. On the phonology of Itza. Odense: English Department, Odense University (36 pp.), quoting and extending Schumann Gálvez 1971:35.
new_statements.locator: section 'Stress', pp. 14-15 (PDF pp. 14-15 of the 36-page scan)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again. (36-page image scan, PDF page N = printed page N) — I read the scanned (the page image) and viewed the page image. The whole quoted passage ('Stress. We have practically no information on the location of stress in Itza. The following citation from Schumann (1971:35).. At any rate we can infer that there is a strong tendency to stress the final syllable of an utterance (be it a single word or a string of words).') is on printed p. 14, word for word (the indented Schumann block included); p. 15 continues with Berendt's accent convention, Stoll 1884:43 ('As a general rule, stress falls on the final syllable..'; German original confirmed at stoll1884 lines 6009-…
new_statements.rule_in_words: In citation form a word is stressed on its final syllable; in connected speech the prominence moves with the intonation of the utterance, but the last syllable of the utterance (word or phrase) is the strong position and emphasis keeps stress final. Dienhart adds from Stoll 1884 and Berendt 1866/67 that all recorded Petén items are final-stressed, that V'V sequences are stressed on the second vowel, and that Spanish loans with non-final stress shift stress to the last syllable (mesa > [meesa'], cofre > [coofre']).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned by Dienhart or Schumann (as quoted). Bennett 2016:497 reports that Hofling 2000:25 describes secondary stress in Itzaj with word-level phonological consequences (not verified here).
new_statements.exceptions: Stress varies in context according to intonation (phrasal conditioning); the rearticulated vowel after a glottal stop (e.g. /ca't/ heard as [ca'at]) 'is never stressed' (Schumann 1971:36-37 via Dienhart p. 17); Spanish loans regularize to final stress with lengthening of the originally stressed vowel.
new_statements.domain_note: Word in isolation (citation form) is final-stressed; in context the domain is the utterance/phrase - Bennett 2016:496 classes Itzaj (citing Schumann 1971, Dienhart 1986, Hofling 2000) with the Q'anjob'al-type phrasally conditioned pattern (phrase-final words final stress, phrase-medial words initial stress); Dienhart does not state the phrase-medial pattern. Dienhart's article is a compilation from Schumann 1971 and 19th-c. wordlists (Berendt, Stoll, Armas, Baezo), not fieldwork.
new_statements.identity_note: Dienhart 1986 writes 'Itza' (Hofling: 'Itzaj'), the Petén/San José variety = itza1241; his data are Schumann 1971 (San José, Petén) plus 19th-century Petén wordlists (Berendt 1866/67, Stoll 1884, Armas 1897, Baezo 1832). No dialect issue. Glottolog's ref #673219 (Burrett 1999, Sipakapense) is a misattribution and irrelevant.

(Middle America chapter; Itzaj Maya example (40) with foot structure, after Hofling 2000:6-8) — and the derived StressTyp2 entry for Itzaj Maya at StressTyp2.ullet.net.
new_statements.locator: StressTyp2 live site: all 846 language rows browsed (?content=browse_language&p=0.16), no Itzaj/Itza/Yucatec/Mopan entry; offline 2015 SQL archive and 2026-09-04 sqlite dump likewise have no Itzaj language, lect or Hofling source. Survey book: Middle America chapter, passage around example (40) 'Itzaj Maya (Hofling 2000: 6-8; foot structure added by ourselves)'; page number not given by the Google Books snippet; the De Gruyter DOI page returned an empty body twice (paywalled).
new_statements.relation_note: Catalog record has an empty rule; the existing statement (Schumann 1971:35 via Dienhart 1986:14-15) gives final stress for words in isolation. The survey (summarising Hofling 2000:6-8) separates domains: lexical stress is root-initial (+ alternating, + heavy syllables) and the final stress is phrasal, overriding word stress at phrase end. This differs from the existing statement in placement at the word level (root-initial vs final) but reconciles it as the phrase-final rule, so 'refines' rather than 'contradicts'.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word-level stress falls on the first syllable of the root and on alternate syllables after it; heavy syllables (VV, V' per Hofling) are stressed wherever they occur; the last syllable of the phonological phrase carries phrasal stress, which overrides word-level stress (so a word in isolation surfaces with final stress). The survey adds foot structure: (à?)(wì.nik)(-é?).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Alternating stresses on syllables after the root-initial one (the survey's feet mark non-final feet with grave accents, the phrase-final syllable with an acute).
new_statements.exceptions: Phrasal stress supersedes word-level stress at the end of the phonological phrase (compare winik 'man' in (40a-c)). The StressTyp2 database has no Itzaj entry at all, so the 'derived StressTyp2 entry' does not exist.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the Itzaj of San José, Petén (Hofling's consultant Tesucún; Schumann's 1971 and 2000 Itzá). The survey book's example is Hofling's data. No dialect split is at issue.

readall_conflicts: Schumann 1971:35 (as quoted by Dienhart 1986:14-15, already in the catalog) says stress always falls on the final syllable when a word is uttered in isolation and varies with intonation in context; Hofling 2000:6-8 (via the van der Hulst et al. 2010 survey snippets and the Google Books snippets of the grammar saved in check2/) says lexical stress falls on the first syllable of the root and on alternate and heavy syllables, while phrasal stress on the last syllable of the phonological phrase supersedes it. The two are reconciled by domain (isolation = a one-word phrase, so the phrasal rule wins), but a catalog reading of 'final' would misdescribe the word-level system; Bennett 2016:496 groups Itzaj with the phrasally conditioned Mayan systems. Schumann 2000 adds nothing on placement (snippets only) and states that Itzá and Mopán lack tone.
